screens.title: What are Pipeline Artifacts?
screens.narratorSegment: Let's start with a fundamental concept: pipeline artifacts. In any complex CI/CD pipeline, jobs often need to share data or results with subsequent jobs. Imagine a scenario where a 'build' job compiles your application's source code into an executable file, like a Java JAR or a Docker image. A later 'test' job then needs that exact executable to run its tests, and a 'deploy' job needs it to push to a server. This is precisely where artifacts come into play. Artifacts are simply files or directories produced by a job that GitLab stores and makes available for download, or for use by other jobs later in the same pipeline. They are absolutely crucial for maintaining a consistent flow of data throughout your CI/CD process. Without artifacts, each job would have to re-run the build step, which is incredibly inefficient, wastes resources, and introduces the risk of inconsistencies if the build process isn't perfectly deterministic every time. Artifacts ensure that the exact same output from one job is used as input for the next, guaranteeing reliability and efficiency. content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Pipeline Artifacts

What are Pipeline Artifacts?

Sharing data and results between CI/CD jobs

Definition: Artifacts

Artifacts are files or directories generated by a CI/CD job that GitLab stores. They are made available for download or for use by subsequent jobs in the same pipeline.

  • •Crucial for maintaining data flow and consistency across pipeline stages.
  • •Prevent redundant work, like re-compiling code in every job.
  • •Ensure that the exact same output is used as input for dependent jobs.
Key Takeaway

Artifacts are essential for efficient and consistent data transfer between jobs, avoiding unnecessary re-execution and ensuring reliability.

Why Artifacts Matter

Scenario: Build & Test

A build job compiles an executable. A test job needs that executable to run tests. Without artifacts, the test job would have to re-compile, wasting time and resources.

Analogy: Assembly Line

Think of an assembly line. Each station (job) performs a task and passes its output (artifact) to the next station. Re-creating parts at each station would be inefficient.

Common Misconception

Some believe jobs automatically share all data. In reality, only explicitly defined artifacts are reliably passed, ensuring controlled and predictable data flow.

screens.title: Defining Artifacts in `.gitlab-ci.yml`
screens.narratorSegment: Now that we understand what artifacts are, let's look at how to define them in your. gitlab-ci. yml file. You use the artifacts keyword within a job definition to specify which files or directories you want to save. The most important sub-keyword here is paths, where you list the specific files or directories that your job produces and that you want to make available. For instance, if your build job compiles Java JAR files, you'd specify the path to those JARs. It's also a best practice to define expire underscore in. This setting automatically removes old artifacts after a specified duration, preventing your GitLab storage from growing indefinitely and becoming a cost burden. Without expire underscore in, artifacts would persist forever, potentially consuming vast amounts of storage. Consider our example: a build underscore backend job compiles a Java application. We use artifacts. paths. to save all compiled JAR files from the build slash libs slash directory. We also set expire underscore in. 1 week to ensure these artifacts are cleaned up after seven days. This simple configuration ensures that the compiled application is available for subsequent jobs, like testing or deployment, without needing to rebuild it, while also managing storage efficiently. This is a fundamental step towards building maintainable and cost-effective pipelines.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Configuring Artifacts

Defining Artifacts in .gitlab-ci.yml

Using paths and expire_in for efficient storage

Key Artifacts Keywords

  • •paths: Specifies which files or directories to save as artifacts. Supports wildcards.
  • •expire_in: Defines how long artifacts should be retained before automatic deletion (e.g., '1 week', '30 days').
  • •reports: (Optional) Used for specific report types like JUnit test reports, making them visible in GitLab UI.
Key Takeaway

Properly configuring artifacts with paths and expire_in is vital for data sharing, pipeline efficiency, and storage management.

.gitlab-ci.ymlExample: Saving JAR files
build_backend:
  stage: build
  script:
    - echo "Compiling Java application..."
    - ./gradlew build
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - build/libs/*.jar # Save compiled JAR files
    expire_in: 1 week # Keep artifacts for 1 week
    reports:
      junit: build/test-results/test/**/TEST-*.xml # Example JUnit report

Common Mistake: Forgetting expire_in

Without expire_in, artifacts accumulate indefinitely, leading to increased storage costs and slower pipeline performance over time. Always define an expiration policy.

screens.title: Explicit Artifact Downloads with `dependencies`
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond simply saving files, artifacts also facilitate dependencies between jobs. By default, jobs in a later stage automatically download all artifacts from all jobs in previous stages. This is an implicit dependency, and while it can be convenient for simple pipelines, it often becomes inefficient as pipelines grow. Imagine a large project with many build jobs in an early stage, each producing large artifacts. If a test job in a later stage only needs artifacts from one specific build job, downloading everything from all previous jobs is a waste of time and bandwidth. This is where the dependencies keyword becomes incredibly useful. You can explicitly list the names of specific jobs from which the current job needs artifacts. This fine-grained control prevents unnecessary artifact downloads, significantly speeding up job execution, especially in large pipelines with many stages and jobs. For example, if you have a deploy job that only needs the artifact from build underscore backend and not build underscore frontend, you can specify dependencies. open square bracket 'build underscore backend' close square bracket. This ensures only the necessary artifact is downloaded, making your pipeline leaner and faster. It's about being precise with your data flow.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Job Dependencies

Explicit Artifact Downloads with dependencies

Fine-tuning artifact retrieval in stage-based pipelines

Understanding dependencies

The dependencies keyword allows you to explicitly list jobs from which the current job needs artifacts. This overrides the default behavior of downloading all artifacts from previous stages.

  • •Default Behavior: Jobs in later stages download ALL artifacts from ALL jobs in previous stages.
  • •dependencies Benefit: Prevents unnecessary artifact downloads, speeding up job execution.
  • •Scope: Works within the strict stage order of the pipeline.
Key Takeaway

Use dependencies to precisely control which artifacts a job downloads, improving efficiency by avoiding superfluous data transfer.

Example: Targeted Artifacts

Scenario: Deploy Job

A deploy job needs the compiled .jar from build_backend, but not the .zip from build_frontend. Using dependencies: ['build_backend'] ensures only the necessary artifact is downloaded.

Misconception: All or Nothing

It's a common mistake to assume you must download all artifacts. dependencies provides a way to be selective, which is crucial for large pipelines.

screens.title: When `dependencies` Limits Parallelization
screens.narratorSegment: While the dependencies keyword offers valuable control over artifact downloads, it's important to understand its inherent limitation: it strictly adheres to the stage order defined in your. gitlab-ci. yml. This means that if you have a build stage, followed by a test stage, and then a deploy stage, all jobs in the build stage must complete before any job in the test stage can begin, regardless of whether a specific test job actually needs artifacts from all build jobs. This creates a linear progression, which can severely limit parallelization. Consider a scenario where job underscore C in stage underscore C needs an artifact from job underscore A in stage underscore A. If job underscore B in stage underscore B also needs job underscore A's artifact, then job underscore B will run after job underscore A and before job underscore C. Even if job underscore C could theoretically run in parallel with job underscore B because their other dependencies are met, the strict stage order forces them to wait. This linear execution can lead to longer pipeline run times, especially in large projects where many jobs could otherwise run concurrently. It's a key bottleneck that dependencies alone cannot solve, pushing us towards more advanced solutions for true parallelization.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Dependencies Limitations

When dependencies Limits Parallelization

The challenge of strict stage order in complex pipelines

The Stage Order Constraint

The dependencies keyword operates within the strict, sequential execution of pipeline stages. All jobs in a stage must complete before any job in the next stage can begin.

  • •Linear Progression: Jobs are forced to wait for previous stages, even if their specific dependencies are met earlier.
  • •Limited Parallelization: This strict order prevents jobs in different stages from running concurrently, even if they are logically independent.
  • •Inefficiency: Can lead to longer overall pipeline execution times, especially in complex projects.
Key Takeaway

While dependencies refines artifact transfer, it cannot overcome the inherent sequential nature of stage-based execution, limiting true parallelization.

Scenario: Linear Bottleneck

Jobs A, B, C across Stages

Job_C (Stage C) needs Job_A's (Stage A) artifact. Job_B (Stage B) also needs Job_A's artifact. Even if Job_C could run in parallel with Job_B, it must wait for Stage B to complete first.

Impact: Slower Feedback

This forced sequential execution means developers receive feedback on later stages much slower than necessary, hindering rapid iteration and deployment.

screens.title: Unlocking Parallelism with DAGs
screens.narratorSegment: To truly unlock parallelization and create more flexible execution graphs, GitLab CI/CD introduces the powerful concept of Directed Acyclic Graphs, or DAGs, using the needs keyword. Traditionally, as we've discussed, jobs in GitLab CI/CD execute stage by stage: all jobs in stage one must complete before any job in stage two starts, and so on. This creates a very linear, sequential flow. A DAG, on the other hand, allows you to define explicit relationships between jobs, regardless of their stage. Think of it as drawing a map of your pipeline where arrows point from one job to another, indicating a dependency, but without any loops or cycles. A job can 'need' another job, meaning the 'needing' job will only start after the 'needed' job completes successfully, and it will automatically download the artifacts from that 'needed' job. The key benefit here is that jobs that don't depend on each other can run in parallel, even if they are in different stages. This drastically reduces overall pipeline execution time, provides much faster feedback to developers, and makes your CI/CD process significantly more efficient and responsive. It's a game-changer for complex projects.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Introducing DAGs

Unlocking Parallelism with DAGs

Overriding linear execution for faster feedback

What is a DAG?

A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a graph data structure where nodes represent jobs and edges represent dependencies, with no circular dependencies. In CI/CD, it defines the execution order of jobs.

  • •Overrides Stage Order: Jobs can define dependencies on other jobs regardless of their stage.
  • •Enables Parallelization: Jobs that don't depend on each other can run concurrently, even across stages.
  • •Faster Feedback: Reduces overall pipeline execution time, providing quicker results.
Key Takeaway

DAGs, implemented with the needs keyword, allow for flexible, parallel job execution across stages, significantly boosting pipeline efficiency.

needs Keyword

Functionality

A job declared with needs will only start after the 'needed' job completes successfully. It also automatically downloads artifacts from the 'needed' job.

Misconception: Just another dependencies

needs is fundamentally different from dependencies. While both handle artifacts, needs breaks the stage barrier, allowing true cross-stage parallelization, unlike dependencies.

screens.title: Implementing DAGs with the `needs` Keyword
screens.narratorSegment: Let's see how the needs keyword brings DAGs to life in a practical example. Consider a common scenario: you have separate jobs to build your frontend and backend, then jobs to test each, and finally a single job to deploy the entire application. Without needs, these jobs would typically be forced into a strict stage order. For instance, all build jobs finish, then all test jobs, then the deploy job. But with needs, we can define explicit dependencies that allow for much greater parallelization. In this example, we define three stages: build, test, and deploy. Notice how run underscore frontend underscore tests explicitly needs build underscore frontend, and run underscore backend underscore tests needs build underscore backend. This means these test jobs can start as soon as their respective build jobs are done, even if other build jobs are still running. They don't have to wait for the entire build stage to complete. Finally, deploy underscore app needs all preceding build and test jobs. This ensures it only runs when all necessary components are ready. This explicit DAG structure allows for maximum parallelization, significantly reducing the overall pipeline execution time and providing much faster feedback to your development team. It's a powerful way to optimize your CI/CD workflow.

keyIdea.title: Cross-Stage Parallelization
keyIdea.text: The `needs` keyword enables jobs to define dependencies on specific preceding jobs, overriding stage order and allowing parallel execution across stages.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Implementing DAGs

Implementing DAGs with the needs Keyword

Defining explicit job relationships across stages

How needs Works

The needs keyword allows a job to explicitly declare dependencies on other jobs, overriding the default stage-based execution order. This enables jobs to run in parallel across different stages.

  • •Job-to-Job Dependencies: Define direct links between specific jobs, not entire stages.
  • •Artifact Transfer: Automatically downloads artifacts from the 'needed' jobs.
  • •Parallel Execution: Jobs can start as soon as their specific 'needs' are met, even if other jobs in their stage or previous stages are still running.
Key Takeaway

needs is crucial for building highly parallelized pipelines, allowing jobs to run concurrently across stages and significantly reducing overall execution time.

.gitlab-ci.ymlExample: Frontend/Backend Pipeline
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

build_frontend:
  stage: build
  script: echo "Building frontend..."
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - frontend/dist/

build_backend:
  stage: build
  script: echo "Building backend..."
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - backend/target/

run_frontend_tests:
  stage: test
  script: echo "Running frontend tests..."
  needs: ["build_frontend"] # Only needs frontend artifacts

run_backend_tests:
  stage: test
  script: echo "Running backend tests..."
  needs: ["build_backend"] # Only needs backend artifacts

deploy_app:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - echo "Deploying app..."
    - ls frontend/dist/ # Access frontend artifacts

    - "run_backend_tests"

screens.title: Parallel Execution in Action
screens.narratorSegment: Let's visualize the power of the needs keyword and how it enables true parallel execution, moving beyond the limitations of strict stage ordering. In our example pipeline, the build underscore frontend and build underscore backend jobs are both in the 'build' stage. Since they don't depend on each other, they can run concurrently. Once build underscore frontend completes, run underscore frontend underscore tests can start immediately, even if build underscore backend is still running. Similarly, run underscore backend underscore tests can begin as soon as build underscore backend is finished. This means both sets of tests can execute in parallel, significantly reducing the overall time spent in the 'test' phase. Finally, the deploy underscore app job, which is in the 'deploy' stage, explicitly needs all four preceding jobs: both build jobs and both test jobs. This ensures that the deployment only proceeds when all necessary components have been successfully built and tested. The beauty of this DAG structure is that it allows independent parts of your pipeline to progress without waiting for unrelated tasks, leading to a much faster feedback loop and a more efficient use of your CI/CD resources. This is a core principle for modern, agile development.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Artifacts and Dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: As you start implementing artifacts and DAGs, it's crucial to be aware of common pitfalls that can lead to inefficient or broken pipelines. One of the most frequent mistakes is not defining expire underscore in for your artifacts. Without this, artifacts accumulate indefinitely, consuming excessive storage and potentially leading to higher costs or performance degradation over time. Always set a reasonable expiration. Another common error is misjudging when to use dependencies versus needs. Remember, dependencies is best for fine-grained artifact control within a strict stage order, while needs is for breaking that stage order to achieve true parallelization across stages. Using dependencies when needs would be more appropriate can lead to unnecessary sequential execution and slower pipelines. Conversely, overusing needs in very simple pipelines where implicit stage order is sufficient can sometimes make your. gitlab-ci. yml more complex than it needs to be. Always consider the data flow and execution order carefully. Finally, be mindful of large artifacts. While artifacts are essential, transferring very large files between jobs can significantly slow down your pipeline due to upload and download times. Only artifact what is truly necessary. By keeping these points in mind, you can design and maintain robust, efficient, and cost-effective CI/CD pipelines.

Module 3›Chapter 3.2›Common Pitfalls

Troubleshooting Artifacts and Dependencies

Best practices for robust and efficient pipelines

Common Pitfalls

  • •Missing expire_in: Leads to excessive storage usage and potential cost increases.
  • •dependencies vs. needs Misuse: Using dependencies when needs would provide better parallelization, or vice-versa.
  • •Large Artifacts: Transferring unnecessarily large files can significantly slow down pipelines.
  • •Over-complication: Overusing needs in simple pipelines where implicit stage order is clearer.
Key Takeaway

Proactively manage artifact expiration, choose the correct dependency keyword, and optimize artifact size to prevent common pipeline inefficiencies and errors.

Best Practices

Define Expiration

Always include expire_in for artifacts to manage storage and keep your GitLab instance lean.

Choose Wisely

Evaluate whether dependencies or needs is appropriate for your specific job relationships and desired parallelization.

Optimize Artifact Size

Only save essential files as artifacts. Minimize their size to reduce transfer times and improve pipeline speed.

Welcome to a crucial chapter in mastering GitLab CI/CD! Today, we're diving into how to make your pipelines not just work, but work efficiently and intelligently. As your projects grow, so does the complexity of your CI/CD pipelines. You'll encounter situations where different jobs need to share data, or where you want to run multiple tasks simultaneously to speed things up. This chapter will equip you with the knowledge of artifacts, dependencies, and Directed Acyclic Graphs, or DAGs, which are fundamental concepts for building robust, fast, and scalable CI/CD workflows. By the end of this lesson, you'll understand how to ensure your jobs get the right data at the right time and how to orchestrate them for maximum parallelization, leading to faster feedback and more reliable deployments. Let's explore how these powerful features can transform your CI/CD strategy.

In this chapter, we'll focus on several key learning objectives that will empower you to build more sophisticated and efficient GitLab CI/CD pipelines. First, you will learn to explain the purpose of artifacts and how to configure them correctly. This involves understanding why sharing data between jobs is essential and how to use the artifacts keyword effectively. You'll also learn to differentiate between the dependencies and needs keywords. These two features control job execution order and data flow, but they operate under different principles, and understanding their distinctions is crucial for pipeline optimization. By grasping these concepts, you'll lay a strong foundation for managing complex CI/CD workflows, ensuring your pipeline jobs communicate and execute exactly as intended. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Building on our foundational understanding, our next objectives will guide you towards designing truly efficient and responsive pipelines. You will learn to design efficient pipelines by leveraging Directed Acyclic Graphs, or DAGs, to maximize parallelization and minimize feedback loops. This involves understanding how to break free from strict stage-based execution and orchestrate jobs to run concurrently whenever possible. Finally, you'll be able to identify common pitfalls related to artifact management and dependency definition in complex pipelines. Recognizing these common mistakes will help you proactively avoid issues, troubleshoot effectively, and build more robust and reliable CI/CD workflows. These advanced skills are vital for any developer or DevOps engineer looking to optimize their deployment processes and deliver software faster. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's start with a fundamental concept: pipeline artifacts. In any complex CI/CD pipeline, jobs often need to share data or results with subsequent jobs. Imagine a scenario where a 'build' job compiles your application's source code into an executable file, like a Java JAR or a Docker image. A later 'test' job then needs that exact executable to run its tests, and a 'deploy' job needs it to push to a server. This is precisely where artifacts come into play. Artifacts are simply files or directories produced by a job that GitLab stores and makes available for download, or for use by other jobs later in the same pipeline. They are absolutely crucial for maintaining a consistent flow of data throughout your CI/CD process. Without artifacts, each job would have to re-run the build step, which is incredibly inefficient, wastes resources, and introduces the risk of inconsistencies if the build process isn't perfectly deterministic every time. Artifacts ensure that the exact same output from one job is used as input for the next, guaranteeing reliability and efficiency. What are Pipeline Artifacts? means artifacts are job outputs saved and shared across pipeline stages, ensuring consistent data flow and preventing redundant work.. In practical terms, sharing data and results between ci/cd jobs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now that we understand what artifacts are, let's look at how to define them in your. gitlab-ci. yml file. You use the artifacts keyword within a job definition to specify which files or directories you want to save. The most important sub-keyword here is paths, where you list the specific files or directories that your job produces and that you want to make available. For instance, if your build job compiles Java JAR files, you'd specify the path to those JARs. It's also a best practice to define expire underscore in. This setting automatically removes old artifacts after a specified duration, preventing your GitLab storage from growing indefinitely and becoming a cost burden. Without expire underscore in, artifacts would persist forever, potentially consuming vast amounts of storage. Consider our example: a build underscore backend job compiles a Java application. We use artifacts. paths. to save all compiled JAR files from the build slash libs slash directory. We also set expire underscore in. 1 week to ensure these artifacts are cleaned up after seven days. This simple configuration ensures that the compiled application is available for subsequent jobs, like testing or deployment, without needing to rebuild it, while also managing storage efficiently. This is a fundamental step towards building maintainable and cost-effective pipelines.

Beyond simply saving files, artifacts also facilitate dependencies between jobs. By default, jobs in a later stage automatically download all artifacts from all jobs in previous stages. This is an implicit dependency, and while it can be convenient for simple pipelines, it often becomes inefficient as pipelines grow. Imagine a large project with many build jobs in an early stage, each producing large artifacts. If a test job in a later stage only needs artifacts from one specific build job, downloading everything from all previous jobs is a waste of time and bandwidth. This is where the dependencies keyword becomes incredibly useful. You can explicitly list the names of specific jobs from which the current job needs artifacts. This fine-grained control prevents unnecessary artifact downloads, significantly speeding up job execution, especially in large pipelines with many stages and jobs. For example, if you have a deploy job that only needs the artifact from build underscore backend and not build underscore frontend, you can specify dependencies. open square bracket 'build underscore backend' close square bracket. This ensures only the necessary artifact is downloaded, making your pipeline leaner and faster. It's about being precise with your data flow.

While the dependencies keyword offers valuable control over artifact downloads, it's important to understand its inherent limitation: it strictly adheres to the stage order defined in your. gitlab-ci. yml. This means that if you have a build stage, followed by a test stage, and then a deploy stage, all jobs in the build stage must complete before any job in the test stage can begin, regardless of whether a specific test job actually needs artifacts from all build jobs. This creates a linear progression, which can severely limit parallelization. Consider a scenario where job underscore C in stage underscore C needs an artifact from job underscore A in stage underscore A. If job underscore B in stage underscore B also needs job underscore A's artifact, then job underscore B will run after job underscore A and before job underscore C. Even if job underscore C could theoretically run in parallel with job underscore B because their other dependencies are met, the strict stage order forces them to wait. This linear execution can lead to longer pipeline run times, especially in large projects where many jobs could otherwise run concurrently. It's a key bottleneck that dependencies alone cannot solve, pushing us towards more advanced solutions for true parallelization.

To truly unlock parallelization and create more flexible execution graphs, GitLab CI/CD introduces the powerful concept of Directed Acyclic Graphs, or DAGs, using the needs keyword. Traditionally, as we've discussed, jobs in GitLab CI/CD execute stage by stage: all jobs in stage one must complete before any job in stage two starts, and so on. This creates a very linear, sequential flow. A DAG, on the other hand, allows you to define explicit relationships between jobs, regardless of their stage. Think of it as drawing a map of your pipeline where arrows point from one job to another, indicating a dependency, but without any loops or cycles. A job can 'need' another job, meaning the 'needing' job will only start after the 'needed' job completes successfully, and it will automatically download the artifacts from that 'needed' job. The key benefit here is that jobs that don't depend on each other can run in parallel, even if they are in different stages. This drastically reduces overall pipeline execution time, provides much faster feedback to developers, and makes your CI/CD process significantly more efficient and responsive. It's a game-changer for complex projects.

Let's see how the needs keyword brings DAGs to life in a practical example. Consider a common scenario: you have separate jobs to build your frontend and backend, then jobs to test each, and finally a single job to deploy the entire application. Without needs, these jobs would typically be forced into a strict stage order. For instance, all build jobs finish, then all test jobs, then the deploy job. But with needs, we can define explicit dependencies that allow for much greater parallelization. In this example, we define three stages: build, test, and deploy. Notice how run underscore frontend underscore tests explicitly needs build underscore frontend, and run underscore backend underscore tests needs build underscore backend. This means these test jobs can start as soon as their respective build jobs are done, even if other build jobs are still running. They don't have to wait for the entire build stage to complete. Finally, deploy underscore app needs all preceding build and test jobs. This ensures it only runs when all necessary components are ready. This explicit DAG structure allows for maximum parallelization, significantly reducing the overall pipeline execution time and providing much faster feedback to your development team. It's a powerful way to optimize your CI/CD workflow.
